overview: Sekisui House is Japan's largest homebuilder, with a core business spanning custom-built detached houses, rental/commercial buildings, architectural and civil engineering, rental housing management, remodeling, condominiums ("Grande Maison") and urban redevelopment. Since 2017 the company has built a large and fast-growing overseas business, principally US homebuilding (via the roughly $5 billion acquisition of M.D.C. Holdings/Richmond American Homes in 2024, combined with Woodside Homes, Chesmar Homes and Holt Homes, all unified under the "Sekisui House U.S." brand in January 2026), plus master-planned community and multifamily development in the US, and residential development in Australia and Singapore. Overseas business now accounts for roughly 30% of consolidated net sales (FY2025: about JPY1.29 trillion of JPY4.20 trillion total), transforming Sekisui House from a pure domestic housebuilder into a globally diversified residential developer.

business_model.summary: Revenue is generated across three broad Japan-domestic business lines (Built-to-Order, Supplied Housing, Development) plus a large and increasingly dominant Overseas Business. Built-to-Order (custom detached houses, rental/commercial buildings, architectural/civil engineering) is largely project/contract-based and cyclical with housing starts. Supplied Housing (rental housing management fees, remodeling) is the most recurring, annuity-like revenue stream, tied to Sekisui House's large installed base of managed rental units. Development (real estate brokerage, condominiums, urban redevelopment) is lumpier, driven by the timing of large property and condominium deliveries. Overseas (primarily US detached-home sales via Sekisui House U.S., plus master-planned community land sales, multifamily development, and Australian/Singaporean residential projects) is now the largest single segment by revenue and has become the main swing factor in consolidated profit.
business_model.customer_type: B2C homebuyers and homeowners (custom houses, condominiums), B2B/institutional landlords and corporate real estate owners (rental housing, CRE/PRE, architectural/civil engineering), and US retail homebuyers through Sekisui House U.S.
business_model.geographic_mix: Japan domestic roughly 69% of FY2025 net sales (Built-to-Order + Supplied Housing + Development segments); Overseas roughly 31% (predominantly US homebuilding/communities/multifamily at ~¥1.18tn, Australia ~¥110bn, plus equity-method Singapore operations).

main_competitors: In the US: D.R. Horton, Lennar, PulteGroup, and fellow Japanese entrants Daiwa House (Stanley Martin, CastleRock, Trumark) and Sumitomo Forestry (DRB Group)
competitive_position.market_position: Japan's largest detached-house builder by sales, with roughly 4% share of total new Japanese housing starts (custom detached, rental, and condominium combined) and a long-standing leadership position in the industrialized/prefabricated housing segment. Through MDC Holdings (Richmond American Homes), the combined Sekisui House U.S. entity ranked as the #6 largest homebuilder in the US by 2024 closings (~14,700 homes, ~$8.1bn gross revenue), making Sekisui House the largest Japanese homebuilder operating in America.

moat_factors.factor: Brand and quality reputation in Japan
moat_factors.description: Decades-long reputation for build quality, structural technology, and after-sales service support premium pricing and strong order backlogs in custom detached houses and rental housing.

In-house design, construction, and a large owned/managed rental housing stock (Sha Maison brand) generate recurring management fee income and cross-sell opportunities (remodeling, brokerage) across the owned customer base.
Leading share of net-zero-energy houses (ZEH) in Japan (96% of detached houses built were ZEH in FY2024) supports differentiation ahead of 2025 Building Energy Efficiency Act mandates.

Acquisitions (MDC/Richmond American, Woodside, Chesmar, Holt) built top-6 US homebuilder scale and presence across major Sun Belt and Mountain West markets, though integration and brand consolidation (completed January 2026) is still recent and unproven at full scale.
Long-term rental housing management contracts and corporate real estate (CRE/PRE) relationships create some switching friction for existing managed-property owners.

weaknesses: Commodity-like US homebuilding economics (incentives, land/lot costs, construction cost inflation) dilute what was historically a premium-branded Japan model
Structurally shrinking core Japanese new-build market (housing starts in long-term secular decline) caps organic growth of legacy segments
Low profitability in the newly dominant Overseas segment (operating margin fell to ~3.0% in FY2025 from 6.2% in FY2024) versus mid-teens margins in several domestic segments
Complex, acquisition-heavy multi-brand US structure carries integration/execution risk even after the January 2026 rebrand to one entity
Thin margins and intense competition in Japan's architectural/civil engineering business

growth_drivers: Transformative growth strategy overseas under the new Seventh Mid-Term Management Plan (FY2026-FY2028): 'Building a Growth Platform to Drive a Game-changing Transformation' abroad, 'Cultivating the Sekisui House Economic Sphere' at home

Integration and brand unification of US homebuilders (MDC/Richmond American, Woodside, Chesmar, Holt) into a single 'Sekisui House U.S., Inc.' entity (completed January 2026) to transfer Japanese technology/brand and capture scale/cost synergies
US master-planned community and multifamily development pipelines, with large land/lot banks (~52,600 lots held or under contract) supporting future home closings

Growth in high-margin, recurring Japan businesses: rental housing management (Sha Maison, PM company launch FY2025), remodeling, and real estate brokerage (newly consolidated into Sekisui House Real Estate)
Urban redevelopment pipeline in central Tokyo, Nagoya, Osaka and Fukuoka (e.g., Grand Green Osaka), a high-margin, if lumpy, profit contributor

Secular tailwind from Japan's 2025 Building Energy Efficiency Act mandate (universal energy efficiency compliance) and Long-Life Quality Housing certification favoring Sekisui House's ZEH/quality leadership
Capital allocation toward overseas investment (overseas capex running roughly 2.5-3x domestic capex in recent years) signaling continued US/Australia expansion
Target of ROE in the high-12% range by FY2028 (vs. 11.3% FY2025) under the new mid-term plan, with a minimum dividend floor of ¥145/share

business.description: FY2025 US homebuilding operating profit swung to a loss (-¥5.3bn/-$35mn) as rising incentives and inventory valuation losses hit margins amid buyer wait-and-see behavior on rates and tariffs.

New housing starts in Japan have fallen from ~974,000 (FY2016) to ~740,000-816,000 in recent years, driven by demographics (shrinking/aging population, household formation decline); Sekisui House's own unit volumes have followed a similar downward trend.

Consolidating MDC Holdings, Woodside, Chesmar and Holt into one 'Sekisui House U.S.' entity (Jan 2026) is operationally complex and unproven; prior roll-up execution (large MDC acquisition cost/integration expense already recognized in FY2024) adds risk.

business.risk: Customer concentration/order-based volatility in architectural/civil engineering and urban redevelopment
business.description: Large project-based segments are lumpy and dependent on timing of government and corporate construction and sale of large redevelopment properties.
Soaring materials and labor costs pressure margins in custom detached houses and architectural/civil engineering, requiring price pass-through that could dampen demand.

financial.description: Interest-bearing debt roughly tripled from ¥775bn (FY2023) to ~¥1.88tn (FY2024/25) to fund the ~$5bn MDC deal; net debt/EBITDA rose to 3.5x and debt/equity to ~88%, versus near debt-free levels (D/E ~37-44%) before the acquisition. Equity-to-asset ratio fell from >50% to ~41-43%.

US business results are translated into yen; a stronger yen (USD/JPY assumed to fall from ~150 to ~145 in FY2026 guidance) is a headwind to reported overseas revenue and profit, while a weaker yen flatters results.

Land and buildings for sale ballooned to ~¥3.03 trillion (FY2025) from ~¥1.18 trillion (FY2021), largely reflecting US land/lot inventory; this is subject to valuation write-downs if demand softens (already seen in FY2025 US inventory losses).
Interest expense increased from ¥3.8bn (FY2021) to ¥39.2bn (FY2025) as debt levels rose, a direct drag on ordinary profit even as operating profit grew.

regulatory.risk: Japan Building Energy Efficiency Act revisions
regulatory.description: Mandatory energy-efficiency compliance for all new homes raises build costs and created demand pull-forward/pull-back distortions around the FY2025 transition, though Sekisui House's ZEH leadership positions it well longer term.
US tariffs on construction materials add cost uncertainty and have been cited by management as a factor behind cautious US homebuyer sentiment and wait-and-see demand.

regulatory.risk: Foreign ownership/antitrust scrutiny of US homebuilder consolidation by Japanese acquirers
regulatory.description: Increasing Japanese ownership of major US homebuilders (Sekisui House, Daiwa House, Sumitomo Forestry collectively ~5-6% of US single-family closings) could draw political/regulatory attention over time, though no specific action is currently pending.

macro.description: US homebuilding demand and margins are highly sensitive to mortgage rate trends; management explicitly cites 'falling mortgage rates' as a prerequisite for the expected recovery in US new home demand.

Japan's shrinking and aging population structurally reduces long-run demand for new detached housing and rental housing construction, a multi-decade drag partially offset by redevelopment, remodeling and overseas diversification.
Management repeatedly flags US tariff policy and geopolitical risk as sources of uncertainty for both the global economy and US consumer sentiment.
Elevated materials and labor costs in both Japan and the US pressure margins across build-to-order and homebuilding segments.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Japan's new housing starts are in secular decline (~740,000-820,000 units/year currently vs. ~970,000 a decade ago) due to demographics, but higher-value-added, energy-efficient and redevelopment/remodeling segments are growing. The US housing market has structural undersupply and latent demand but near-term starts remain soft on affordability/rate uncertainty; a recovery is expected as mortgage rates ease. Japanese homebuilders (Sekisui House, Daiwa House, Sumitomo Forestry) have become major consolidators of the US homebuilding industry, collectively approaching ~5-6% of US single-family closings.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - both Japanese and US new-home order/construction volumes are sensitive to interest rates, consumer confidence, and broader economic cycles; the Development (urban redevelopment, condominiums) and US homebuilding segments are the most cyclical, while rental housing management and remodeling are comparatively defensive/recurring.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - directly affects US homebuyer affordability/demand and mortgage-dependent Japanese buyers; also affects Sekisui House's own elevated post-MDC debt service costs (interest expense up roughly 10x since FY2021).
key_input_costs: US tariffs on imported building materials

recent_developments.event: FY2025 (fiscal year ended January 31, 2026) results: consolidated net sales ¥4.198tn (+3.4% YoY), operating profit ¥341.4bn (+3.0%), profit attributable to owners ¥232.1bn (+6.6%); results exceeded the original Sixth Mid-Term Management Plan targets despite a sharp overseas profit decline.

Completed 'One Company' integration of US homebuilders: M.D.C. Holdings (renamed Sekisui House U.S., Inc. in September 2025), Woodside Homes, Chesmar Homes and Holt Homes unified under a single operating structure, ending separate brand operations.

Formulated the Seventh Mid-Term Management Plan (FY2026-FY2028): 'Cultivating the Sekisui House Economic Sphere' domestically and 'Building a Growth Platform to Drive a Game-changing Transformation' overseas; targets ROE in the high-12% range by FY2028 and a minimum annual dividend of ¥145/share through the plan period.

US homebuilding segment swung to an operating loss (-$35mn/-¥5.3bn) as the company raised sales incentives amid buyer caution and recorded inventory valuation losses, driving overall Overseas Business operating profit down 50.5% YoY to ¥39.1bn despite flat overseas revenue.

FY2026 (ending January 2027) guidance: net sales ¥4.353tn (+3.7%), operating profit ¥350.0bn (+2.5%), ordinary profit ¥314.0bn (-4.2%), profit attributable to owners ¥218.0bn (-6.1%); overseas operating profit expected to recover to ¥56.5bn (+47.3%) while domestic development/urban redevelopment profit is guided down from an unusually strong FY2025.
Annual dividend raised to ¥144/share for FY2025 (from ¥135) and guided to ¥145/share for FY2026, continuing a multi-year streak of dividend increases with a payout ratio policy of 40%+.

Japan housing starts continued to soften (total starts down from ~820,000 to ~793,000-816,000 range), with a pull-forward/pull-back pattern around the Building Energy Efficiency Act revision affecting owner-occupied and rental housing starts.

guidance.as_of: FY2025 (fiscal year ended January 31, 2026) results announcement, March 5, 2026

items.vs_prior: raised (implies +3.7% YoY growth on FY2025 actual of ¥4,197,922mn)
items.notes: Growth driven by continued overseas expansion (overseas sales guided to ¥1,428,000mn, +11.0%) and domestic built-to-order/supplied housing growth; development segment sales guided down (-9.1%) on tough urban redevelopment comp.
Operating margin guided to 8.0%, down slightly from 8.1% in FY2025, reflecting margin recovery overseas offset by normalization in development segment margins.
Decline driven by absence of the large FY2025 equity-method gain (¥26.1bn) and continued elevated interest expense on post-MDC debt.

items.metric: Profit attributable to owners of parent / EPS
items.notes: Net margin guided down to 5.0% from 5.5% as non-operating items normalize.

items.vs_prior: raised sharply vs. FY2025 actual ¥38,348mn (+47.3% YoY)
items.notes: Recovery predicated on stabilizing US incentive levels and improved homebuilding profitability; overseas revenue guided to ¥1,428,000mn (+11.0%).
Management set a minimum annual dividend floor of ¥145/share for the entire Seventh Mid-Term Management Plan (FY2026-FY2028) with a target payout ratio of 40%+ (FY2026 guided payout ratio 43.1%).

Seventh Mid-Term Plan (FY2026-2028) total investment plan is ¥56,000mn (100 millions of yen, i.e. ¥5.6 trillion-equivalent in the stated unit) with overseas investment (¥3,750 in 100-millions-of-yen units, i.e. ~¥375bn-equivalent scaled) continuing to run well above domestic capex.

items.period: FY2028 (final year of Seventh Mid-Term Management Plan)
items.vs_prior: raised medium-term target vs. FY2025 actual ROE of 11.32% and FY2026 guided ROE of 10.1%
items.notes: Management explicitly frames FY2026 as a trough/transition year for ROE within the new plan, targeting recovery to the high-12% range by FY2028 as overseas margins normalize and the balance sheet deleverages.

guidance.management_commentary: Management describes the global economy as 'increasingly uncertain' due to US tariff policy and geopolitical risk, with Japan's housing market past its energy-efficiency-law demand rush and the US market still in a 'wait-and-see' phase pending clarity on mortgage rates and tariffs. CEO Yoshihiro Nakai's Seventh Mid-Term Management Plan (FY2026-2028) sets 'transformative growth' in the US (via the newly unified 'Sekisui House U.S.' entity) alongside 'stable growth' leveraging group-wide capabilities in Japan, while financial strategy explicitly balances growth investment, 'restoration of financial soundness' (i.e., deleveraging after the MDC acquisition), and shareholder returns, including a ¥145 minimum dividend floor and flexible share buybacks tied to the pace of balance-sheet repair.

bull_case: Transformed into a top-6 scale US homebuilder (via MDC/Richmond American, Woodside, Chesmar, Holt, now unified as Sekisui House U.S.) giving exposure to a structurally undersupplied US housing market with long-run demand tailwinds once rates ease

Diversified, now ~31%-overseas revenue base reduces dependence on Japan's demographically shrinking new-build market, with overseas profit guided to recover sharply (+47%) in FY2026 off a depressed FY2025 base

High-margin, recurring domestic revenue streams (rental housing management ~9.7% margin and growing, remodeling ~14-15% margin) provide earnings stability and benefit from Sekisui House's large owned/managed housing stock

Consistent, growing shareholder returns: dividend raised for multiple consecutive years to ¥144 (FY2025) with a ¥145 floor set through FY2028, 40%+ payout policy, and flexible buybacks as leverage normalizes
New Seventh Mid-Term Management Plan targets ROE recovery to the high-12% range by FY2028, with explicit management focus on deleveraging the balance sheet after the large MDC-funded debt increase
bear_case: US homebuilding profitability has deteriorated sharply (FY2025 operating loss in the core US homebuilding sub-segment) as incentives rise and buyers stay on the sidelines amid rate/tariff uncertainty, with recovery dependent on macro factors outside management's control

Leverage increased materially to fund the ~$5bn MDC acquisition (net debt/EBITDA ~3.5x, debt/equity ~88% vs. ~40% pre-deal), leaving less balance-sheet flexibility and higher interest costs just as overseas earnings have weakened
Japan's core new-housing-start market is in secular decline on demographics, structurally capping growth in custom detached houses and limiting the scope of the largest heritage business lines

FY2026 guidance implies declining ordinary profit (-4.2%) and declining profit attributable to owners (-6.1%) even as revenue grows, reflecting margin compression and normalization of one-off development/equity-method gains

Complex, multi-brand US roll-up (four distinct builders integrated into one entity only as of January 2026) carries real execution risk, and currency translation (yen/dollar) adds volatility to reported overseas results
